groups.title: Browser Security
groups.question: Your app shows user comments with formatting, and you find that someone posted a comment that ran a script in other users' browsers. Explain how this happened and how you would protect forms that change data too.

followUps.Cross-site scripting: React escapes text by default, so how can an XSS bug still happen?
followUps.CSRF and SameSite cookies: What is a CSRF attack, and how do SameSite cookies help?

evidence.text: Cross-site scripting runs an attacker's script on your page with your users' permissions.
React escapes text, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML, unsafe links like javascript URLs and third-party scripts bypass it.
Any HTML from users must be sanitized before it is rendered.

misconceptions.text: Says React apps cannot have XSS.

evidence.text: In CSRF, another site makes the user's browser send a request that carries their logged-in cookies.
SameSite cookies are not sent on most cross-site requests.
Anti-forgery tokens prove that the request came from your own page.

notEnough: Only saying CSRF is a forged request.

groups.title: Headers and Policies
groups.question: Your security team asks for a Content Security Policy, and a developer says CORS already protects the API. Explain what each of these does and what it does not do.

followUps.Content Security Policy: How does a Content Security Policy limit the damage of an XSS bug?
followUps.CORS: Why is CORS not a replacement for checking who is allowed to use your API?

evidence.text: A CSP header lists where scripts, styles and connections are allowed to come from.
Injected scripts from other sources or inline scripts are blocked by the browser.
It reduces the impact of an XSS bug even when one exists.

notEnough: Only saying CSP is a security header.

evidence.text: CORS lets a server tell browsers which other origins may read its responses.
It is enforced by browsers, so tools like curl or other servers ignore it.
The API must still check authentication and permissions on every request.

notEnough: Only saying CORS controls cross-origin requests.

misconceptions.text: Says CORS stops attackers from calling your API.

groups.title: Auth and Dependencies
groups.question: Your app stores a long-lived token in localStorage and uses 300 npm packages nobody has reviewed. Explain the risks and what you would change.

followUps.Storing tokens: Why is a long-lived token in localStorage risky, and where should it go instead?
followUps.Dependency risk: Why is every npm package a security risk, and how do you manage it?

evidence.text: Any script on the page can read localStorage.
A single XSS bug can steal the token and give the attacker the session.
HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies keep session credentials out of JavaScript's reach.
Each package runs with the same access as your own code.
Review what you add and pin versions with a lockfile.
Automated audits and security updates catch known vulnerable versions.

notEnough: Only saying to run npm audit.

groups.title: Build and Ship
groups.question: A developer put an API secret in a VITE_ environment variable, and releases are deployed by hand from a laptop. Explain how the build works and how you would ship safely.

followUps.What Vite does: Why must a secret never be stored in a VITE_ variable?
followUps.CI/CD and monitoring: What should a pipeline do between a push and a production deploy, and how do you learn about errors afterwards?

evidence.text: In development Vite serves source files as native modules, and for production it bundles them.
Variables starting with VITE_ are written into the browser bundle.
Anything in the bundle can be read by any user, so secrets must stay on the server.

notEnough: Only saying not to commit secrets.

misconceptions.text: Says environment variables are hidden from users because they are not in the source code.

evidence.text: The pipeline runs lint, tests and a build on every push.
A preview deploy lets the change be reviewed before it is merged and deployed.
Error monitoring reports failures real users hit after release.
